newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Japan telecom firms make new push into Asia.
newsitem.headline: Japan telecom firms make new push into Asia.

text.p: Japanese electronics firms, defeated by European and American rivals in the early 1990s, are making another assault on the Asian telecommunications market, this time boosted by mighty ally NTT.

NEC Corp and Fujitsu Ltd, dominant at home, and others such as Hitachi Ltd and Oki Electric, are rushing into Asia, where demands for telecoms systems are doubling every year thanks to deregulation and competition.
In Thailand, Singapore, the Philippines and Malaysia, deregulation is spawning new second carriers and they are seeking foreign partners, finance and technologies.
"NEC's business in Asia will be a lot different in the next few years," Iwao Shinohara, NEC's Associate senior executive vice-president told Reuters in an interview.
"Not to mention changes in the business climate, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp's (NTT's) entry into international services is a big advantage to us," he said.

Shinohara said Japanese equipment makers had been seriously handicapped by NTT's absence because carriers and equipment makers usually go hand-in-hand in overseas projects, using the same format and technology.

Others also said partnerships with carriers was vital for equipment makers to get into the global market because they are often required to provide financing, equipment and telecoms operations in a package to win contracts.

NTT, after 14 years of wrangling with the Japanese government, was freed to pursue international business in January in return for an agreement to split itself into four units under a holding company.
Since then, NTT has been seeking business on the global market, joining with others to seek carrier licences in Singapore and Hong Kong, among others.
Japanese telecom equipment makers are also focusing on new technologies of wireless phone systems and an advanced switch system called ATM (asynchronous transfer mode) in Asian markets.

"By the time we tried to sell cellular phone handsets in Asia, the European GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) phone standard had dominated the market," said Takashi Sekizawa, President of Fujitsu Ltd.
"We lost out in a format war in the first stage, but we will be able to compete with European and American rivals on level playing fields in the areas of new technologies," he added.
Fujitsu aims to raise its telecom sales in the Asia-Pacific region to 95 billion yen ($830 million) in the year ending March 31, 1998, up from 64 billion yen a year earlier.
NEC, on the other hand, plans to increase its telecom sales in China, including those from chips and computers, by 25 percent to around 140 billion yen during the year.
Since early this year in China, NEC has acquired a majority share in a pager company, opened a giant digital switch plant and an integrated chip production plant.
It aims for Chinese sales of $2.2 in 2000.
